A neighborhood in limbo: Woodland Park residents organize amid redevelopment plans

Sand Hill Property Company looks to transform East Palo Alto neighborhood
by Lisa Moreno August 21, 2026 7:56 amUpdated August 22, 2026 8:53 am
  • Share on X (Opens in new window) X
  • Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook
  • Print (Opens in new window) Print
  • Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email

Instaread

Roland Guidry moved to East Palo Alto as a child in 1962, two decades before it officially became a city.

He attended the now shuttered Ravenswood High School. He met his wife in the city. People were friendly, left their doors unlocked and local agencies were nearly “handing out” housing, he said in an interview. 

But over time, the environment changed. 

When Guidry had moved to Woodland Park in the 1980’s, the neighborhood, nestled between U.S. 101, Menlo Park and Palo Alto, was in the midst of a tug-of-war between local agencies who wanted to acquire the land. The early conflict presented a window to the future, when real estate companies would fight to develop the area. 

For decades thereafter, Woodland Park apartments have remained an island of affordability in a region where real estate prices have escalated to unprecedented heights. While neighboring cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park have consistently struggled to meet their goals for affordable housing, the neighborhood west of the highway has been sheltering many of the region’s service workers, academics, immigrants and young professionals. The sprawling apartment buildings just across the creek from Palo Alto’s affluent Crescent Park neighborhood have been bought and sold numerous times in the last two decades, but the neighborhood’s status as a bastion of rental housing remained intact.

In that time, the quality of the buildings diminished, Guidry said. Residents have endured pest infestations, mold, mass evictions and even a property manager that suddenly vanished in 2009, leaving offices vacant and buildings in disrepair. 

Across various interviews with this publication, residents said they stay because of affordability, proximity to loved ones and because East Palo Alto is home. But residents have long anticipated redevelopment. Many have wondered when a developer will take the jump to transform Woodland Park and potentially force them to find housing elsewhere.

A Peninsula property company’s recent pitch to demolish and renovate hundreds of units in the neighborhood have revived those fears. Sand Hill Property Company, East Palo Alto’s biggest landlord, is planning to demolish nearly 500 units and build over 1,000 more, even as current tenants continue to fight the company for better living conditions. Residents and advocates contend the development could force people out of the city and drastically change the community. 

The plans, which are now advancing through the city’s development pipeline, are stirring fears of displacement among longtime residents. Guidry has made friends and raised his kids in Woodland Park. He and wife, who recently underwent major surgeries, want to be close to their doctors at Stanford. But like many of his neighbors, he feels uneasy about prospective development. 

Guidry envisions a stressful move out of the city he’s called home for decades should plans to demolish his building unfold. 

“This could be a gated community,” Guidry said. “Where are people going to go?”

A legacy of affordability

One of East Palo Alto’s first priorities as a new city in 1983 was to protect residents from displacement and rising living costs in the region. In the years that followed, it created some of the most stringent tenant protections and affordable housing restrictions in the county and state (see this story for a history of Woodland Park). 

But today, the sentiment has changed among newer residents and council members, some of whom argue that the local laws have inhibited housing and city development. 

Mayor Webster Lincoln and Council members Mark Dinan and Martha Barragan recently expressed support for changing the city’s Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, a local law that requires developers to allocate 20% of new on-site rental units to affordable housing for residents who earn 35%, 50% and 60% of the average median income, which is approximately $114,000. If the units are for sale, 20% of them must cater to median to moderate income levels. Developers may also pay an “in-lieu” fee if they do not wish to include the units. 

The proposal, which narrowly failed to advance last month, could have temporarily slashed the number of required affordable units under current city laws. 

Residents and local advocates protested the possible changes, and believed that the proposal was antithetical to the city’s early mission to protect residents from displacement. 

The conflict underlined a growing rift between longstanding council members Carlos Romero and Vice Mayor Ruben Abrica, who were both in the frontlines of East Palo Alto’s incorporation effort and who sought to keep the area affordable, and newer ones, like Lincoln, Dinan and Barragan, who have expressed commitment to producing new housing and promoting economic development. 

With Abrica and Barragan’s seats up for grabs in an upcoming election, the council dynamic could change in a crucial way. New electeds will get a chance to revise the city’s inclusionary-housing requirements and review a significant housing proposal slated for the west side. They will also have a chance to shape a question that has been on the minds of the city’s largest residential neighborhood since its inception: What will happen to Woodland Park?

On the precipice of change

Despite being only 107 acres and 8% of East Palo Alto’s land, the west side of East Palo Alto houses approximately 22% of the city’s residents, according to the city’s General Plan. 

The west side’s Woodland Park neighborhood, much of which has been managed by a single property owner since 2007, contains 95% of the city’s rent-controlled housing, according to the plan. Sand Hill Property Company, which purchased more than 1,800 Woodland Park units in 2016, still manages a large mass of the neighborhood today. 

In late 2025, Sand Hill submitted preliminary applications to demolish dozens of Woodland Park residential buildings to make way for new ones across two projects titled O’Keefe-Manhattan and West Bayshore-Newell Improvements. 

After hosting a pre-application community meeting and soliciting early feedback from East Palo Alto’s Planning Commission, which weighed concerns over gentrification with the need for housing, Sand Hill submitted formal plans for the two projects in April and June this year. 

Under the O’Keefe-Manhattan project, the development company proposed to renovate 221 existing rental units, demolish 344, construct 114 for-sale townhomes and build 736 new apartment units. The nearby businesses Launderland and La Tiendita Market would also be demolished. 

Sand Hill proposed to distribute the townhomes across 21 new buildings between Euclid Avenue and Manhattan Avenue, and the rentals across four apartment buildings along West Bayshore Road and East O’Keefe Street. 

The company also hopes to create approximately 1,400 parking spaces in the project area but did not specify how they would be allocated. Renovated units across both projects would receive added carports, updated kitchens, flooring and paint. The West Bayshore-Newell plans included proposals to renovate 315 existing rental units, demolish 144, build 391 new apartment units and 60 for-sale townhomes, as well as 2,800 square feet of retail space. Three Brothers Tacos and a 7-eleven would also be torn down. 

Sand Hill would then construct 10 townhome structures along Newell Road and a large segmented apartment complex near the intersection of West Bayshore Road and Newell Road (a list of addresses where renovation and demolition is proposed can be found here).

Residents have protested prospective development for over a decade in Woodland Park, expressing concerns over displacement and reduction of affordability in the largely rent-controlled area. Previous Woodland Park landlords contributed to those concerns by drastically spiking rents, issuing arbitrary late rent fees and evicting tenants. According to a UC Berkeley housing study, the now-defunct company Page Mill Properties, which at one point served as Woodland Park’s largest landlord, evicted people at a rate 7.5 times greater than the rest of San Mateo County. 

Sand Hill maintains that it wouldn’t displace any residents over the course of development. The company plans to replace all existing rent-controlled units one-for-one and lock in the below-market rents of existing tenants, spokesperson Christie Farrell wrote in a message.  

“All existing tenants will always be able to stay at Woodland Park,” Farrell wrote. “They will be relocated to other Woodland Park units during construction and have the right to remain at their same rent-stabilized rents.” 

Even so, the company has already taken steps to reduce its obligation to provide affordable units. In recent months, it has expressed interest in submitting an application that would reduce the affordable units it has to build under East Palo Alto’s Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, according to city documents.  

The City Council tentatively planned to discuss the projects on May 19, according to City Manager Melvin Gaines, but the conversation was delayed. As of June 5, the agenda-setting committee did not solidify a date to evaluate the projects, Gaines said. 

Although it is unclear when the project would roll out or what it will look like when it does, Sand Hill representative Mike Kramer predicted the planning process would be long. 

“We expect construction to be phased and take many years,” Kramer told the city’s Planning Commission during an April meeting. 

Sand Hill’s other housing proposals may provide a glimpse into the planning process for the  O’Keefe-Manhattan and West Bayshore-Newell Improvements.

The company first proposed in 2019 to develop a section of the west side in a project titled Woodland Park Euclid Improvements. After approximately three years of deliberation, the council gave Sand Hill the green light to demolish 161 existing units to make way for 605 new multi-family units. 

Since then, Sand Hill has been sluggish to begin construction after demolition, leaving two vacant lots in the project zone, and residents who had hoped to to return to their units in temporary housing. 

The company has also shifted its plans for below-market housing. In lieu of following the city’s affordable-housing requirements, Sand Hill originally agreed to contribute approximately $23 million to develop 78 affordable housing units at 851 Weeks Street in partnership with Eden Housing, according to the city. 

But in early July, Sand Hill made a new deal with the city to contribute up to $14 million toward a Ravenswood City School District affordable-housing project containing 430 units. 

Citing rising construction costs and interest rates, Sand Hill contended it was too difficult to follow through with its original plans.

This wasn’t the first time that Sand Hill has pivoted in its housing plans. 

In September 2025, Lincoln, Dinan and Barragan approved Sand Hill’s proposal to slash the amount of affordable for-sale housing units and omit all very low-income units from the “Four Corners” housing project at 1675 Bay Road without paying an in-lieu fee. 

City staff and consultants had recommended against the proposal, calling it a “significant loss in public benefit,” after the company had spent approximately six years planning with the city. 

Council member Dinan, who campaigned on a desire to develop the city, said he has philosophical differences with longstanding council members who have sought to sustain the inclusionary housing ordinance in its full capacity. He believes the strict affordable housing protections actually end up blocking low-income housing production. 

Without the restrictions, Dinan said that building more housing would lower the rent rates across the city. 

“No one wants to swim with a 100-pound weight on their back,” he said in an interview. 

Dinan also contended that the outdated multi-family housing in Woodland Park, where residents often report mold and broken appliances, contribute to negative health impacts, he said. 

“We need to replace this unsafe housing,” he said. 

Fighting for improvements

Sand Hill’s assurances to East Palo Alto leaders about their ambitious plans for Woodland Park have done little to sway many of the existing tenants, some of whom have been battling the company over living conditions. Jose Perez has been living in Woodland Park apartments for 26 years, and his family’s quality of life has never been as bad as it is today, he said. 

Standing in his single-room unit, his wife Neli Perez, urged him to pull up his sleeves to show the condition of his skin, which was covered in red, irritated splotches. Her legs looked the same, covered in welts. 

The bug bites started when Sand Hill finally replaced their old carpet with flooring that he contended was not new, Jose Perez said. Management would not acknowledge their multiple requests for help and at one point blamed them for the pests. 

Even after building fumigation, they’ve been dealing with the painful bites for three years now. 

“I don’t know what to do anymore,” he said in Spanish. “I don’t have hope.”

The Perez’s complaints are familiar in Woodland Park, said local tenant organizer Angelica Hernandez, who stood outside her apartment in late July. In fact, she has experienced many of the same issues as the tenants she helps represent. 

At night, Hernandez’s family wears earplugs to protect themselves from cockroaches, and her countertops are stained yellow from multiple fumigation attempts, she said. At one point, maintenance left a massive hole in the wall under her sink, allowing pests to travel from unit to unit, she said, no matter what she did to keep them away. 

But her decision to stay in the neighborhood is easy, because she’s working to organize her fellow neighbors with the Regional Tenant Organizing Network. 

The Bay Area advocacy group became fully acquainted with East Palo Alto renters in 2024, after Woodland Park tenants heard rumors that Sand Hill was planning to sell some of its properties. They then agreed to organize, said network Director James Huynh. 

The East O’Keefe Tenant Association was born in collaboration with residents of 201, 245 and 301 East O’Keefe Street, who eventually submitted a formal rent relief petition to the East Palo Alto Rent Stabilization Board. 

Since its early days, the tenant association has expanded to include 300, 340, 355, 360 and 380 East O’Keefe Street. Tenant advocates have increased efforts to help residents learn their rights and embark on the long process to formally report the property company for poor living conditions. 

Huynh said the main goal is for residents to have a say in their future in Woodland Park. 

“The rights of tenants are being violated, and there is a large company that owns a monopoly of properties in East Palo Alto and properties all across the Bay Area, who refuses to really engage face-to-face with the people who pay them rent every month,” Huynh said. 

The pitches to demolish and build new properties in Woodland Park have brought increased urgency to the tenants’ mission: to directly establish a consistent line of communication between residents and company executives. They’ve received no response from company founders, Peter and Susanna Pau, Huynh said. 

“If they want to redevelop the whole community, they have to talk to the association first,” Huynh said. 

Well after the initial residents founded the tenant association and had filed formal complaints over the rat and cockroach infestations, severe mold and broken appliances, Sand Hill sold all three of the buildings. Kramer of Sand Hill told this publication that the sales were executed “for typical business reasons.”

The rent board granted the tenants’ restitution in May 2025, stating that management had “unreasonably” delayed repairs and did not adequately address pest problems 

Residents of 201 E. O’Keefe St. were granted a 7% rent reimbursement from Sept. 2021 through May 2025, and a 5% rent reduction from June 2025 through May 2026. 

Tenants at 245 E. O’Keefe St. were awarded a 5% monthly rent reimbursement from Sept. 2021 through May 2025. They were also granted a 5% rent reduction from June 2025 to May 2026. 

Tenants at 301 E. O’Keefe St. were granted a range of rent reimbursements from 7% to 22% for approximately two years, depending on their specific living circumstances. They were also entitled to a continuous award if elevator malfunctions and leaky pipes persisted after the hearing, according to city documents. 

Sand Hill spokesperson Farrell said that community engagement staff and a pest control management company have remedied complaints from various properties throughoutin Woodland Park. The company has hosted six in-person meetings with tenant organizers, but the company founders are not directly involved with the East Palo Alto portfolio, she wrote. 

“Woodland Park Apartments is overseen by a third-party property manager, Asset Living,” Farrell wrote in a message. “Any complaints or work orders they receive, they look into and address.”

Sand Hill appealed each of the decisions, asserting that it should not have to fix conditions that have “existed for many years,” according to city documents, and that some residents had moved out during the relief period. Although Sand Hill has not paid any of the residents, the East Palo Alto rent board recently doubled down on its rent relief approval for 201 East O’Keefe St. 

“There were notes in the appellant’s response around not agreeing with anything that was awarded and wanting to throw out all of it,” Board member DeVan Taylor said at an August 12 meeting. “I’m not inclined to do that.”

Board members unanimously directed city staff to clarify the dates in which each resident lived in the building, and to prorate their reimbursement accordingly. They also asked staff to extend the rent relief period for the dates residents were not paid. 

Leading up to the announcement, residents anxiously sat in the crowd, some covering their mouths in anticipation, others seemingly reserved after a long day of work. 

But by the end of the August 12 meeting, the room was quiet as most residents had left before the late-night decision. 

In the months leading up to the appeal hearing, tenants had participated in dozens of meetings to learn their rights and plan protests against Sand Hill. 

One demonstration, at a Menlo Park Residence Inn owned by Sand Hill, drew police activity after residents called on hotel staff to connect them with the company’s founders, the Paus. Dozens of residents stood inside the lobby on June 3, holding signs reading phrases like “release our money.” 

Police officers, one of whom honked in support of the protest while peeling away, asked protesters to stand outside of the building. There, new members of the tenant association spoke about their experiences in Woodland Park. 

“I hear the landlord is planning to demolish buildings and rebuild them, but they can’t afford to pay these tenants. … Stop the appeals, invest in our homes, stop the plans to displace us,” Guidry said in a speech, drawing applause. 

A week after the action, the day finally came for residents of 201 East O’Keefe to participate in their own appeal hearing, which was scheduled for June 10. But East Palo Alto staff suddenly cancelled their hearing on the day it was supposed to happen. Disappointed residents were asked to wait until the August meeting for their hearing. 

Residents of 245 and 301 East O’Keefe Street are still waiting for a verdict.

A list of addresses where Sand Hill is planning new developments can be found here.
